wa_mount_constance_north_chute.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, then up Avalanche Canyon past the South Chute
wa_mount_constance_north_chute.notes:
Bike or walk the closed Dosewallips Road (FS 2610) about 5 miles to the Lake Constance climbers' trail, then the steep, unmaintained trail roughly 3,300 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camp at the north end of the lake.

From the lake, head north into Avalanche Canyon. This route is the parallel couloir further into the canyon: where the standard South Chute line turns east and climbs out early, the North Chute keeps you in the canyon bed longer and climbs from higher up it.

It sees less traffic than the South Chute and is commonly used as one half of a loop — up one, down the other — rather than as a route in its own right. It rejoins the standard line where the South Chute's gully tops out, crosses the Finger Traverse (or the Terrible Traverse when conditions allow), and finishes over the summit block and the North Chimney.
wa_mount_constance_north_chute.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow in the chute is an improvement on the scree, but Avalanche Canyon is named for what runs down it in May and June
hazards: Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes is called out explicitly for May-June conditions
A long, loose gully with rockfall onto anyone below
It leads to the same exposed upper crossings as the standard route: the Finger Traverse ledge, or the Terrible Traverse's steep snow above a cliff
Less traffic means less boot track and fewer people to ask
wa_mount_constance_north_chute.baseFinding: The whole route-finding problem on this route is telling this chute from the other one, and the test is: keep walking up the canyon past the first chute. The published instruction for the South Chute is to start climbing east as soon as the Cat Ears tower is visible, and trip reports describing this line say plainly that you bypass the South Chute entrance and continue up loose talus to the mouth of the North Chute further into Avalanche Canyon. So the discriminator is temporal, not visual: the first opportunity to leave the canyon eastward is the wrong one. In cloud, where the Cat Ears cannot be seen at all, this is still workable because the test is about the canyon floor under your feet rather than about a skyline. From the lake, follow the canyon north. Do not turn uphill at the first gully. Keep going on the talus until the canyon delivers you to a second, more northerly couloir, and take that. The confirming test is at the top of the chute: it narrows and eases, and the summit block comes into sight to the north for the first time. Just above, a narrow exposed ledge trending left meets the point where the South Chute's loose gully comes in from below. From there the two routes are the same line: north through a notch, across a snowfield, then the Finger Traverse (a downsloping ledge with a horizontal finger crack and old pitons), or the lower Terrible Traverse, the steep exposed snow crossing above a large cliff, when conditions allow. Honest limit: this chute is documented mostly as a variation inside other parties' loops. It is long, loose and less travelled, and there is no marker sequence inside the gully itself.

wa_mount_constance_north_chute.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
wa_mount_constance_north_chute.notes: The alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail. Road-walk or bike roughly 6.5 miles from the washout past the Lake Constance turn-off to the road end at the old campground and ranger station, then the Constance Pass Trail south and southwest to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin, and climb to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass drop south into upper Avalanche Canyon. This is the variant that suits this route best of the three Constance routes, because the North Chute is the higher of the two chutes and coming in from Crystal Pass you meet it without walking the whole canyon up from the lake.
hazards: Unmarked cross-country between Constance Pass and Crystal Pass on talus, scree and lingering snow
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Avalanche and rockfall in the canyon and the chute
Commits to the exposed Finger or Terrible Traverse at the end of a long approach day
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end
wa_mount_constance_north_chute.baseFinding:
This is the one approach where the North Chute is the easy one to find, because you arrive above it. Dropping into Avalanche Canyon from Crystal Pass on the intermittent climbers' path, the first couloir that offers a line up onto the Constance side is the North Chute. Take it. If you keep descending the canyon you will next pass the Cat Ears and the Thumb and eventually reach the South Chute entrance and then the lake — every one of which means you have gone below the route.

The confirming test is the same as on the lake approach: near its top the chute narrows and eases, the summit block comes into sight to the north, and a narrow exposed ledge trending left meets the point where the South Chute's gully joins from below. Above that the line is shared with the standard route and crosses the Finger Traverse, or the Terrible Traverse when conditions allow.

Honest limit: the climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass, so this variant's own approach is the navigationally hard part, not the chute.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: Cathedral Pass and Peggy's Pond, then the east ridge and Lynch draw

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond, below Cathedral Rock
bivy.notes: The base for Mount Daniel and the eastern option for Mount Hinman, and by a distance the most convenient high camp on this side of the divide. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac roughly eleven to twelve miles of rough, narrow gravel to the Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end, take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up to the pass near 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft directly under Cathedral Rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly step that is a genuine obstacle for some parties under an overnight pack. From the pond the standard Daniel route takes the southeast ridge between Circle Lake and the permanent snowfield to the saddle below the east summit at about 7,899 ft and on to the true summit at 7,959 ft, the highest point in the Alpine Lakes; the Lynch Glacier on the north side is the historic line and has shrunk sharply in recent years, draining into Pea Soup Lake. Hinman from here is the less direct half of its two approaches — it means traversing the northeast slopes of Daniel at around 5,300 ft to Pea Soup Lake, crossing to its west end, dropping to about 5,500 ft and then climbing southwest to the summit — long, and much easier under continuous snow than on late-season talus. The Necklace Valley side is the shorter way to Hinman; come here when Daniel is the objective, or when you want both. The critical 2026 caveat: the Cle Elum River road and the Cathedral Pass trail have been inside a fire-area closure running from mid-August to the end of October, along with the campgrounds along that road, so the entire eastern approach has been shut for the back half of the season. Confirm the closure has lifted before driving out — it is a four-hour round trip from the Foss side to find out the hard way.
bivy.water: The pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it, reliable through the normal season. Squaw Lake, about 800 ft lower on the trail in, is the fallback and the overflow camp.
bivy.permit: This is the most restricted camp in the zone and the rules are the point. Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Campfires are prohibited outright — the pond is well above the fire-ban line, the basin is fragile and badly worn, and there is no wood. Party size is reduced here: plan on eight rather than the usual twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group that size. Camp only on the existing hardened pads; areas posted as closed for restoration are legally off limits and staying in one is a violation, not a discourtesy. Do not build wind blocks or fire rings — this is the single most common damage in the basin. Move on rock rather than heather. The spur trail is hiker-only, so no stock.
bivy.capacity: Small and strictly limited. Roughly four or five levelled bivouac pads plus a marginal sloping one, and several of the larger areas that used to be camped have been flagged for restoration and are closed. It fills, and there is no honest overflow inside the basin.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Cathedral Rock Trailhead (Cle Elum River Road)

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes:
Hike the Cathedral Rock Trail to Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) at 2.5 miles, continue to Cathedral Pass at 5,550 ft, then turn left (west) onto the PCT. In less than half a mile turn right (northwest) onto Trail #1375 — do not follow the PCT down toward Deep Lake. Follow #1375 past Cathedral Rock to Peggy's Pond at about 5,560 ft and camp there. This is the shorter approach with the longer summit day, and it avoids the brush of the alternative.

From camp, climb to about 6,300 ft on the east ridge, then traverse below the Daniel Glacier at 6,100 to 6,300 ft toward Lynch draw.

Trailhead to camp is about 2.5 to 4 hours; camp to summit 5 to 7 hours.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.season: Jun-mid Jul, while Pea Soup Lake is frozen and the moat closed; the lake crossing gets hard once it melts
hazards: Full-width crevasses opening late in the season across the Lynch Glacier
Loose, rotten rock on the ground used to gain and leave the ice, reported as the worst hazard on the route
A moat at the rock-to-ice transition that widens through the summer
Pea Soup Lake melting out and Lynch draw flooding from mid-July
Glacier recession changes conditions year to year; old descriptions understate rock and moat work
Short exposed scrambly step on the spur to Peggy's Pond under an overnight pack
Cathedral Pass trail and Cle Elum River road under fire-area closure in late season
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.baseFinding:
The arrival test is a lake you walk across. Traversing below the Daniel Glacier you come to Lynch draw and, in season, to frozen Pea Soup Lake. Walk straight across it and get onto the ice above the low rocks on its far side. That is the base of the Lynch Glacier, and standing on the lake surface is an unambiguous confirmation you are in the right basin.

What to do when the lake has melted out, which is the common case from mid-July: do not try to force the draw, which can be flooded. Instead climb the ridge separating the Daniel and Lynch glaciers for a couple of hundred yards to the first minor notch at about 6,600 ft. Drop roughly 100 ft off it to a snowfield hugging the ridge, then work climbers' left via a second snowfield and rock benches onto the Lynch Glacier. First minor notch at 6,600 ft, then down 100 ft and left: that is a counted sequence rather than a described one, which is what you want in cloud.

Getting onto the ice, in either season: early, take the snow finger on climbers' right. Late, bypass on climbers' left by class 3 scrambling, and expect a moat at the transition. The loose rotten rock used to reach the ice is repeatedly reported as more dangerous than the glacier itself.

And the top tells you which summit is which: the glacier leads to the gap between the two highest summits. From the notch, the west summit — on your right — is the true high point. Late in the season expect a detour around crevasses about two thirds of the way up.

A scope note that matters to peak-list parties: reaching the upper Daniel Glacier from Peggy's Pond by the Southeast Ridge or the Hyas Creek Glacier is a scramble and is not this route.

wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.name: Deception Pass, Marmot and Jade Lakes, and Dip Top Gap from the east
camps: Hyas Lake and Upper Hyas Lake
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.notes:
From the Deception Pass trailhead, hike to Marmot and Jade Lakes and continue to Dip Top Gap. From the gap, traverse west to the shoulder overlooking the Foss River drainage, then descend to the outlet of Pea Soup Lake.

This is the longer, eastern line into the same basin. It reaches the Lynch Glacier at the same point the Peggy's Pond approach does, and everything about identifying the ice is identical from the lake outlet onward.
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.season: Early season, roughly June into July, before the moat opens
hazards: Crevasses across the full width of the glacier late in the season
A moat at the rock-to-ice transition
Loose, rotten rock on the class 3 bypass; rockfall risk
A long approach over Dip Top Gap with a descent to the lake that must be reversed on the way out
Glacier recession changes conditions year to year
wa_mount_daniel_lynch_glacier.baseFinding:
You are aiming for the outlet of Pea Soup Lake, and the shoulder above the Foss River is the waypoint that gets you there. From Dip Top Gap the traverse is west until you are on the shoulder looking down into the Foss River drainage; the descent from that shoulder lands at the lake outlet. If you are looking down into a drainage that is not the Foss, you have not traversed far enough west.

From the outlet the finding is the same as from Peggy's Pond: get onto the ice above the low rocks at the head of the lake. Early season, take the snow finger on climbers' right; late season, bypass by class 3 on climbers' left and cross the moat. Then ascend the upper glacier toward the West Pyramid and the col between the Middle and True summits.

The negative test: this route is graded third class with only minor snow and ice difficulty. If you are on steep ice, you are not on the Lynch Glacier standard line.

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Upper Trailhead on NFR 24, Trail #812 summer route
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes:
From the Upper Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24 / FS 2419 — vault toilet, picnic table, Northwest Forest Pass required — Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is stacked stairstep switchbacks through forest, merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft.

From the merge, continue up the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline at about 4,500 ft, roughly a mile in. In summer conditions the trail is snow-free and well cut essentially to the top, switchbacking across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes to the 5,944 ft summit. Total gain from the Upper Trailhead is 2,444 ft over 1.6 miles one way. No water on the upper route; carry all you need.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.season: Roughly Jul-Oct for the snow-free summer trail; outside that the chute fills and the upper switchbacks are buried
hazards: Southeast-facing snow chute is an avalanche funnel, sun-soaked and prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog
Losing the trail under snow leads onto steeper, looser ground
Very popular trail with kicked-loose rock from parties above
No water on the route; carry all you need
Aggressive, human-habituated mountain goats near the summit
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.baseFinding:
The decision point on this mountain is a signed junction at timberline, roughly 4,500 ft, and a sign is the best fog marker there is because it does not depend on visibility beyond arm's length. At that junction the winter climbing route breaks right, straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, and the maintained summer trail switchbacks left across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly meadows. This variant is the left one.

If you find yourself climbing a single steep funnel-shaped gully rather than working a series of switchbacks, you have taken the right-hand branch and you are on the winter route.

Second test, higher: the summer trail threads a narrow notch and then crosses west-facing slopes before the final approach to the summit. Many of its switchbacks have stairstep risers built into them. Built steps are man-made and unambiguous underfoot. If you are on trackless scree you have left the trail.

Honest limit, and it is seasonal rather than navigational: outside roughly November to June, snow fills the chute and buries the upper switchbacks, and most parties then climb the chute directly because the summer trail is not there to be found. That is not a route-finding failure; it is a different route, and it demands an ice axe and traction. The rocks in and bordering the chute are notoriously slick when wet even outside full winter conditions — that is an official Forest Service warning, not a trip-report opinion.

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: Lower Trailhead, the long approach to the same trail

bivy.name: Big Creek Campground, Lake Cushman
bivy.notes: The obvious roadside base for Mount Ellinor and Mount Washington, sitting at the junction where the Lake Cushman road becomes FR 24, with FR 2419 climbing from there to the Ellinor lower trailhead at about 2,600 ft, the upper trailhead at about 3,500 ft, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the road end near 3,000 ft. Both peaks are genuine day objectives — Ellinor is a maintained trail and Washington a class 3 scramble through a basin and gully — so this is explicitly a contingency rather than the normal plan: it exists for the party that arrives the night before to get an early start on a hot day, or that comes down from the Washington gully later than intended and would rather not drive. It is also the sane base for anyone linking the Washington–Ellinor ridge traverse, which takes far longer than either peak alone. A trail from the campground connects up toward the Mount Ellinor system if you want to walk the whole thing from the tent, but that turns a half-day into a very long one.
bivy.water: Seasonal potable water is generally available in the campground, but do not count on it outside the main summer season. Big Creek runs alongside
bivy.permit: Per-night Forest Service fee. No wilderness permit — this is a developed campground on Forest Service land, outside the national park. Vault toilets, tables and fire rings, pack it in and pack it out. Note the separate parking rule up the hill: a Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Mount Ellinor upper trailhead but not at the lower one, and the Mount Washington trailhead at the end of FR 2419 follows the Forest Service pass regime as well
bivy.capacity: A large forested loop campground — published site counts vary between roughly two dozen and considerably more, so check current numbers rather than trusting a figure. Sites are well spaced in second growth

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes:
The Lower Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft, 3.1 miles one way, and takes no fee. It welcomes you with an easy grade rather than the upper trailhead's near-immediate jolt, and it is the sensible choice when FS Road 2419-014 to the upper lot is snowed in or gated.

It climbs steadily through forest and joins the upper-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. Everything above the merge is identical.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.season: Roughly Jun-Oct, and it is snow-free earlier than the upper road in some years
hazards: The 3,900 ft merge with the upper trail is where parties descend to the wrong trailhead
Southeast-facing snow chute above timberline is an avalanche funnel, prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog
Losing the trail under snow leads onto steeper, looser ground
No water on the upper route
Aggressive, human-habituated mountain goats near the summit
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.baseFinding:
The first test is the merge at about 3,900 ft, where the lower trail joins the upper-trailhead trail. From below, that junction is the confirmation you are on the right path at all; from above it is the fork you take downhill to get back to the lower lot rather than the upper one. Parties have descended to the wrong car here.

The decision point is the same signed junction at timberline, roughly 4,500 ft, about 2.5 miles from the lower trailhead: the winter climbing route breaks right up the chute, the summer trail switchbacks left. Take the left.

And the same confirmations above it: stairstep risers built into the switchbacks, a narrow notch, and west-facing slopes before the summit.

wa_mount_ellinor_standard.name: The winter chute, direct from the timberline junction
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.notes:
Not a different trailhead but a genuinely different climb, and it is what most parties are on outside core summer because the summer switchbacks are buried. From either trailhead, follow Trail #812 to the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and take the right-hand branch straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute below the summit saddle.

This demands an ice axe and traction — crampons or microspikes — and it is steep, funnel-shaped slide-path terrain with real avalanche potential. Check avalanche conditions before going up.

It is also the fast descent when conditions allow: with an axe carried in self-arrest position, parties glissade roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes. That is consequential terrain rather than a casual slide.
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, while the chute holds a firm continuous snowpack
hazards: A steep funnel-shaped slide path with real avalanche potential; check NWAC before going
Wet-slide danger by early-mid afternoon in spring on a sun-soaked southeast aspect
Exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute as snow thins — glissading then becomes dangerous
An uncontrolled glissade or a fall on hard snow without self-arrest skill on genuinely consequential terrain
Slick chute-bordering rocks when wet or in fog
wa_mount_ellinor_standard.baseFinding:
The base is the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and the right-hand branch out of it. That is the whole test and it is the same sign the summer parties turn left at. The chute is the prominent scree-and-snow funnel that runs straight up toward the summit saddle from there — there is one, it is obvious, and it is the reason the junction is signed at all.

The confirming test is that the ground stops switchbacking. The summer trail traverses; the chute goes up the fall line. If you are still zig-zagging you took the left branch.

The test for whether you should be there at all, which matters more on this route than finding it: the chute is south-east facing and sun-soaked, and by early-to-mid afternoon in spring it is prone to wet slides. Start early. Later in the season, as the snow thins and exposes talus, rock and ice bulges, the chute stops being the fast line and becomes the dangerous one — at that point the correct call is the summer switchbacks for the whole descent.

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. All three ways in converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must drop about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing runs through avalanche terrain earlier than that
hazards: Route-finding is the crux: Fernow is not visible from Leroy Basin and cairns are sparse
About a thousand feet of descent from the col into the Gloomy basin that must be regained on the way out
Open crevasses and icy slopes at the Gloomy Glacier remnant; rope up or give it a wide berth
Avalanche terrain on the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing earlier in the season
Roughly two thousand feet of exceptionally loose talus and scree above the basin
Exposed gravel-covered sloped slab traverse (about 30 m drop) and narrow exposed ledges off the col; avoidable
Exposed class 4 (occasionally low 5th) moves on the final summit block
Afternoon thunderstorms on the open upper ridge
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.baseFinding:
Fernow is not visible from Leroy basin, and this is confirmed rather than folklore. Parties climbing the basin under the cirque of Seven Fingered Jack report having real difficulty identifying the route because the peak simply is not in view. Do not stand in the basin trying to pick your line off the mountain; you cannot see it. Carry a track.

The arrival test is short and physical: cross the moraine below the Gloomy Glacier, go up the waterfall, and you are in the broad basin below Fernow. That is where the climbing starts.

Above that basin there are two decision points and both have a wrong answer that is on record.

First: descend the glacier to its terminal moraine at about 6,500 ft, then climb the right side of a stream to an upper snow-filled basin, and from there go south-west up a broad gully that turns eastward. That is Class 2-3 and gives you the luxury of knowing where you are. The alternative — dropping only to 7,000 ft and making a rising traverse through a succession of gullies, ribs and small cliffs — is Class 3-plus with snow and ice and the feeling of being lost somewhere in the Entiat Mountains.

Second, and this is the one that matters: from the broad gully, do not go all the way to the col and traverse the south-east face on the narrow ledges there. They are described as exposed enough to frighten a bird, with the honest observation that a fallen body would be unlikely to be found. Instead climb the broad gully to about 8,400 ft, then a loose gully to about 9,000 ft, and traverse the face at nine thousand on a wide ledge that is not exposed at all.

The 8,400 ft mark is a real landmark rather than a number on a map — two independent parties record the ground changing character there, one of them at a large bench holding permanent snow with water running off it. From 8,400 the line goes up loose talus to the ridge between Seven Fingered Jack and Fernow, where cairns pick up and weave around to the south-east ridge of the summit block. The cairns are reported by three separate parties, though one notes they stop near the summit itself.

The general principle behind all of it: climb as far as you can up the ridge separating Fernow's south-east and south-west faces. Once on the East Ridge, a couple of hundred feet of Class 3 on reasonably solid rock finishes it.

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.name: Holden Village and Copper Basin
wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.notes: From Holden Village up to the Copper–Entiat divide and the east ridge. The most direct way to the standard east-side line, and climbable in a day from Holden, but it depends on the Lake Chelan boat. The ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly than the Leroy Basin approach.
hazards: Loose scree and talus throughout the upper basin and on Fernow itself
Rockfall in gullies and benches, worse with other parties above
Exposed, unavoidable class 4 (occasionally low 5th) moves on the final summit block
Complex cross-country route-finding on the final approach
Afternoon thunderstorms on the open upper ridge
Boat-dependent access via Lake Chelan to Holden

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.name: Entiat River from Cottonwood

approachLogistics.trailhead: Entiat River Trailhead (Cottonwood, end of Entiat River Road)

wa_mount_fernow_southeast_face.notes: Up the Entiat River trail toward the Entiat Glacier and the east ridge. The longest way in, with less gain and little avalanche exposure. It reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier.
hazards: Longest way in, with a long Entiat valley walk before the glacier
Entiat Glacier crossing; crevasses and glacier recession can change conditions (unconfirmed for this variant)
Loose scree and talus throughout the upper basin and on Fernow itself
Rockfall in gullies and benches, worse with other parties above
Exposed, unavoidable class 4 (occasionally low 5th) moves on the final summit block
Complex cross-country route-finding on the final approach

wa_mount_fricaba_standard.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake and Constance Pass
wa_mount_fricaba_standard.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,880 ft at the end of FR 2870, follow Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 south along the Dungeness River. The first mile is mostly flat; stay left at the Royal Basin Trail junction near a mile. Camp Handy — riverside meadow with a cedar shingle shelter — comes at about 3.4 miles.

Just past Camp Handy the trail forks; take the uphill fork and begin a sustained, largely switchback-free climb of about 3 miles and 1,800 ft to Boulder Shelter at 6.4 miles and about 4,890 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the whole approach — treat it as the last sure fill-up. Bear right at the shelter onto the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail. The park boundary is about a mile beyond, after which brush closes in from both sides.

The final 2.9 miles to Home Lake at 5,330 ft, roughly 9.3-9.6 miles from the trailhead, climb another 700-900 ft through subalpine forest into heather meadows, crossing two or three small streams; one waterfall crossing is awkward to keep feet dry and is slick with a full pack early season. Home Lake is the standard basecamp for Fricaba, Hal Foss, Mystery and Deception.

From camp continue on climbers' paths — no maintained tread — up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, then traverse and descend west into upper Deception Basin.
wa_mount_fricaba_standard.season: Roughly Jul-Oct per NPS guidance for the Constance Pass and Home Lake corridor; earlier trips should expect lingering snow
hazards: Extremely shattered rotten shale with real rockfall and ankle-turn hazard the whole way up
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes, with the steepest 500-600 ft immediately off the pass
Lingering steep snow on the Constance Pass to Deception Basin traverse into July, warranting an axe
Brief exposed Class 3 downclimbing near the ridge crest and col on the way out
A long, committing backcountry approach far from help
Boulder Shelter sits at the foot of an avalanche chute with snapped trees in the scar
wa_mount_fricaba_standard.baseFinding:
The base of the climb is the col between Fricaba and Hal Foss, and the published test for it is the one thing about this peak that works without seeing anything: from Deception Basin, ascend eastward aiming for the lowest point in the ridge connecting Fricaba with Hal Foss. Lowest point. Not the nearest gully, not the most obvious scree fan — the lowest saddle on that connecting ridge. In cloud you can still tell which way a skyline sags by walking toward the direction the ground stops climbing soonest.

Second test, once at the col: turn away from Hal Foss and follow the ridge up to Fricaba. The North and SW ridges are the two most readily ascended and this is the SW one. The first 500 to 600 vertical feet off the pass is the steepest part of the climb; after that it eases into a straightforward scree hike. So the shape of the effort is a check on the line: steep first, easy after. A route that stays uniformly moderate is not this one.

Third test, and it is which summit: Fricaba's SW peak is the true, higher top. The NE peak lies about half a mile away along the NE ridge and is noticeably lower. If you have walked half a mile of ridge from the top you reached and are now standing somewhere higher, you were on the NE peak.

What the ground feels like, so it does not read as a wrong turn: Fricaba is extremely shattered, rotten shale. Two steps up and one slide back is the normal experience, not evidence you are off route. Brief Class 2-3 scrambling appears near the ridge crest.

wa_mount_fricaba_standard.name: Royal Basin and the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
wa_mount_fricaba_standard.notes:
The other way into the same basin, and the one that suits a party doing Fricaba alongside Mystery and Deception. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead take Trail #833.2 about a mile and bear right onto the Royal Basin Trail #832 at the fork just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the basecamp; upper Royal Basin camps sit around 5,800-6,200 ft.

From upper Royal Basin climb the moraine and a 35-40 degree snowfield to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend scree to the grass and heather benches above Deception Basin. Fricaba is then across the basin to the east.

One published day-2 description of this side has parties angling up toward the pass going east for Fricaba, then round to the left of some gendarmes and up a steep scree route the account calls self-explanatory.
hazards: A 35-40 degree snowfield below the Royal-Deception notch, wanting an axe outside late season
Shattered shale and scree on Fricaba itself
Gendarmes on the approach ridge that must be skirted rather than climbed
Long approach with the last dependable water at Royal Lake
wa_mount_fricaba_standard.baseFinding: Same base, same test, approached across the basin rather than down into it: from Deception Basin, ascend eastward aiming for the lowest point in the ridge connecting Fricaba with Hal Foss. The extra test this side needs is the gendarmes on the way up: the usual line goes round them to the left, then up steep scree. If you are scrambling over towers rather than skirting them, you have taken the crest instead of the scree. And the same summit test: the SW peak is the true top. The NE peak, half a mile off along the NE ridge, is lower. Honest limit: the scree route above the col is considered self-explanatory, which means there is no known marker for it. It is a walk-up on rubbish rock; the navigation problem is getting to the col, not what happens above it.

wa_mount_hopper_standard.name: First Divide from the Duckabush and Marmot Lake

bivy.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
bivy.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

wa_mount_hopper_standard.notes: The historic Skokomish approach is closed by fire damage, and so is this one where it leaves the Duckabush: the park lists the Home Sweet Home Trail, from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide, closed for the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire with no reopening date (trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. When it reopens, the way in is the long Duckabush valley over Big Hump to Marmot Lake, then back to the Home Sweet Home junction and over First Divide. Roughly double the old distance and firmly a multi-day trip with a camp at the lake or at Home Sweet Home.
hazards: Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, no reopening date
Long Duckabush valley approach, largely off-trail and unbridged on the Marmot Lake alternate
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall along the closed corridor
Many similar gullies and ribs below the summit rockwall; wrong lines wall up
Snow choking the summit gully well into summer; ice axe advisable
Loose talus and steep meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Rockfall onto anyone below in the gully system
Very long, remote walk-out far from help
wa_mount_hopper_standard.baseFinding: First Divide is a distinct saddle with Duckabush and Steel to the west and Hopper to the east, and the old climbers' way to the peak splits off here. Do not expect to find it — that tread has been under brush for more than a decade, so treat the saddle itself as the base of the off-trail travel and navigate rather than follow. From the divide, angle east through forest and brush and pop out into open summit meadow, then climb talus toward the rockwall below the top. The identification that actually matters is up there, not at the saddle: several gullies and ribs seam that wall and every one of them looks plausible from the bottom. The one that goes is the line that keeps laying back into short climbable steps; anything that walls up into a blank corner above you is the wrong one, and the honest expectation is that you may back off one and try another. Note a feature at the foot of whichever gully you commit to, because picking it out again from above is harder than finding it from below. The final crest narrows and is impassable in places, so choose your line early.

wa_mount_hopper_standard.name: Staircase and the North Fork Skokomish to First Divide
camps: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
wa_mount_hopper_standard.notes: The historic and shortest way in. From Staircase, follow the North Fork Skokomish trail up the valley to Home Sweet Home and on to First Divide, where the scramble leaves the trail. Fire damage has affected this corridor, so check the park's trail status before planning.
hazards: North Fork Skokomish Trail closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, no reopening date
Rockfall, treefall and landslide hazard in the burn scar along the Staircase corridor
Deep, swift ford of the river at Nine Stream Camp in high snowmelt or heavy rain
Brushy, steep trail between Two Bear Camp and First Divide; abandoned Hopper Way tread lost under brush
Many similar gullies and ribs below the summit rockwall; wrong lines wall up
Snow on the approach and in the summit gully into early summer
Loose talus and steep meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Very long, remote wilderness approach far from help

wa_mount_howard_south_slope.name: Merritt Lake Trailhead and Nason Ridge Trail to Crescent Lake
camps: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
wa_mount_howard_south_slope.notes: The shorter and more direct way in. From the highway turn onto the rough forest road — high clearance is worth having — and drive to the Merritt Lake Trailhead. Climb the Merritt Lake trail to the lake, then join the Nason Ridge Trail and follow it east to Crescent Lake, which sits below the peak's south side. Water is available at Crescent Lake but is unreliable higher on the mountain, so fill there. The trail is well defined the whole way to the lake, and everything above it is your own route-finding.
wa_mount_howard_south_slope.season: July into October once the ridge clears; snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring.
hazards: Wrong-drainage risk: several small bowls resemble the south face and one is the Royal Creek drainage
Boot path leaving the ridge trail northward leads to the neighbouring summit, not this one
No established route above Crescent Lake; route-finding is entirely your own
Loose, dirty Class 3 gully through the cliff band, unreliable holds in both directions
Off-trail talus and brush with slippery grass and dense alder low on the face
Water unreliable above Crescent Lake; remote, no confirmed cell coverage
wa_mount_howard_south_slope.baseFinding: Make sure you are in the right drainage before you climb — several little bowls look like this face, and the one to your east is Royal Creek. That is the single mistake worth guarding against here, and it is made before you gain any height. From the northeast side of Crescent Lake, take the talus field at the head of the lake, directly below the obvious cliff band; a short thrash through woody brush leads to an upper talus field, and from there drift right to get around the cliff. Several gullies break the band and there is no single correct one — parties pick the easiest-looking line and find it loose, dirty Class 3 for about a hundred feet. That crux band is the confirmation you are on the face, not a sign to retreat, but it is unpleasant to reverse, so note your line. Above it the ground eases onto talus and dirt climbers' paths to the top. Note also that a well-worn boot path leaves the ridge trail heading north on the way in: that is the climbers' route to the neighbouring peak and not the way to this one.

wa_mount_howard_south_slope.name: Rock Mountain Trailhead via Rock Lake and the Rock–Crescent col

bivy.name: Crescent Lake
bivy.notes: The base camp for both Mount Howard and Mount Mastiff, and the natural halfway house on the crest traverse. It sits on the Nason Ridge trail one and three tenths miles beyond Rock Lake, reached by traversing a loose slope around the intervening ridge and dropping about five hundred feet, or from the other direction three and a half miles west of Merritt Lake. From the lake the south slope route on Howard goes around the northeast side and straight up, skirting trees and slide alder to a rock band that is passed by any of several easy scrambling gullies onto a large bench; from the bench you can go directly up the south flank to Howard's summit or traverse east onto the southeast ridge. Mastiff stands a mile east of Howard along the crest and almost everyone who camps here takes both in one day. This is a genuine overnight destination rather than pure contingency — the two summits together are a long push from any trailhead in a day, and sleeping at the lake turns a grim outing into a good one. Bugs are heavy through June and early July, and the approach from either end holds snow on the north-facing traverses well into summer.
bivy.water: The lake plus several small running streams in the immediate surroundings, which is unusually generous for this ridge and is exactly why parties fill their bottles here before going up. It is dependable through the season. Everything above the lake is dry, so the four quarts you want for a summit camp or a long crest day come from here.
bivy.permit: None — no wilderness, no permit, no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires above 5,000 feet, which includes this lake, and expect a total burn ban most of the summer.
bivy.capacity: Lakeside sites for a handful of tents, quieter than Merritt because it takes real effort to reach from either direction; use the existing spots rather than clearing new ground on the vegetation

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

bivy.name: Mount Howard summit-area bivouac
bivy.notes: Strictly a contingency and a preference, not a plan. Mount Howard is a day objective from a camp at Crescent Lake and there is no practical reason to haul water and a bag two thousand feet higher except to be on the crest at sunset and dawn, or to be positioned for a full ridge traverse taking in Mastiff to the east and Rock Mountain to the west in one push. It has been done and it works, but it commits you: there is no water, no shelter, no escape from wind, and the descent to the nearest water is a real drop. The route up from Crescent Lake goes around the lake's northeast side and directly up the slope, threading trees and slide alder to a rock band that is turned by easy scrambling gullies onto a broad bench, and the summit is straight up the south flank from there. In spring the upper slopes hold soft snow over a firm base and are booted rather than climbed, with crampons useful on the way down; that is the season a summit camp is most often chosen, and it is also when the exposure up here bites hardest.
bivy.water: None, and no prospect of any. Every drop comes up from Crescent Lake, roughly two thousand feet below, and a party planning to cook and sleep here has historically carried something like four quarts each. Late-lying snow patches on the north side can be melted in early season and are gone by midsummer.
bivy.permit: None — non-wilderness, no permit and no quota. No pass is required at the Rock Mountain or Merritt Lake trailheads; Nason Ridge is the one fee trailhead on this crest, at $5 a day or $30 a year. No campfires, and there is nothing up here to burn. Leave no constructed platform behind; the crest vegetation and thin soil do not recover.
bivy.capacity: One or two people on scraped benches just below the summit. There is no flat ground for a tent, no shelter of any kind, and nothing you would call a site — this is bare ridge crest and you are making a ledge, not finding one.

wa_mount_howard_south_slope.notes: The longer and more scenic way in, and the one commonly used by parties who want the neighbouring summit in the same outing. From the highway near the milepost, climb the Rock Mountain trail to Rock Lake — snow persists above about 5,000 ft into late spring on this side — then cross the col between the two peaks and descend roughly five hundred feet on the far side to Crescent Lake. From there the climb is the same as from the other trailhead. It costs a substantial descent that has to be regained on the return, which is the price of the extra ground it covers.
wa_mount_howard_south_slope.season: July into October. Snow lingers above about 5,000 ft into late spring and the col holds it longest.
hazards: About 500 ft descent from the Rock-Crescent col to Crescent Lake that must be regained on the way out
Snow persisting on the col and above ~5,000 ft on Rock Lake side into late spring
Wrong-drainage risk: several small bowls resemble the south face
Loose, dirty Class 3 gullies through the cliff band above the lake
Off-trail talus and brush above the lake; remote, no confirmed cell coverage
Long day made longer by the added distance; water unreliable above Crescent Lake
wa_mount_howard_south_slope.baseFinding: Crescent Lake is the common starting point, and on this side you arrive at it from above. Cross the col between the two peaks and descend several hundred feet on the far side to the lake; the tell that you are on this variant rather than the direct one is that you reach the water losing height rather than gaining it. From the lake the climb is identical, and so is the mistake to guard against: several little bowls in this basin look like the peak's south face, and being sure of the drainage before you start upward matters more than anything higher on the route. Take the talus field at the head of the lake directly below the obvious cliff band, push through the woody brush to an upper talus field, then drift right to get round the cliff. Several gullies break the band, none of them the single correct one; expect about a hundred feet of loose, dirty Class 3 in whichever you choose. Above it, talus and dirt climbers' paths lead to the summit.

wa_mount_lago_south_slope_south_face.name: From Robinson Creek over Robinson Pass
camps: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
wa_mount_lago_south_slope_south_face.notes: Lago is the highest peak in this group and the least loved underfoot, being a large pile of loose rock where the whole ascent asks for deliberate movement rather than any technique. Camp is normally Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin, reached along the Middle Fork Pasayten, either over Robinson Pass from the low Robinson Creek trailhead or down the Whistler Cutoff from the high start at Slate Pass, with an awkward crossing of upper Eureka Creek when it is swollen with snowmelt. From camp the round trip is a half day. Many parties link straight over to Carru by the connecting col rather than descending and re-climbing, and the southwest slope is a common variation for coming down since it avoids some of the steeper upper rock ribs.
hazards: Notoriously loose, crumbly rock throughout the upper mountain; rockfall onto parties stacked below
Enormous cliff on the north side of the summit ridge
Difficult crossing of upper Eureka Creek when swollen with snowmelt
Open talus and crest give no shelter from thunderstorms
Unmarked cross-country travel; lingering early-season snow in couloirs
Grizzly and black bear country; food storage required
wa_mount_lago_south_slope_south_face.baseFinding: Everything about this climb is on the south side, and the base can be picked up from either of two places. Coming across from the Carru col at about 7,600 ft, the start is where the col's flattish talus stops being flat and tips up into the peak's southwest face, a mixed slope of scree, talus and occasional patches of solid rock with no path, no cairns and no single obvious line, which is itself the signature of this face. Coming up from Shellrock Basin, the start is the toe of the broad south slope above the last stunted trees, at the point where heather gives out and continuous rock begins. In both cases the confirming feature is what is not there: this side carries no cliff band across it. If you are looking up at a wall rather than a long, tedious, uniform slope, you have drifted round onto the wrong aspect and should traverse back south. The mountain's real hazard sits on the far side of the crest, so the top is where care is needed rather than the base. The north side of the summit ridge is an enormous cliff, and the moment you can see straight down you have gone too far north. Which of the crest's several rises is the true high point is not obvious from the face below, so gain the ridge first and judge from up there; a faint boot-worn line runs along the crest and following it is more reliable than picking a top from the slope.

wa_mount_lago_south_slope_south_face.name: From Slate Pass down the Middle Fork Pasayten

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes Mount Carru and Mount Lago short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. What you pay for the position is water and weather. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for Mount Carru, Mount Lago or Lost Peak actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

road.name: Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) and Slate Peak Road (FR 5400-600)
road.status: Narrow, steep gravel with few turnouts above the end of the pavement; no trailers. The 2026 Ptarmigan Fire burned into the Middle Fork Pasayten, and its closure shut the Buckskin Ridge and Eureka Creek trails this approach uses; check the Methow Valley Ranger District's alerts before you go, and expect burned forest and blowdown in the valley.
road.driveNote: From SR 20 at Mazama, follow Lost River Road to the end of the pavement and continue on the gravel Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) to Harts Pass. At the guard station turn right onto Slate Peak Road (FR 5400-600) and drive about 3.5 miles to the Slate Pass Trailhead at the second switchback beyond the horse loading area.
road.seasonalGate: Usually snow-free and open July to September

trip.approach: From the Slate Pass Trailhead (about 6,900 ft), take Buckskin Ridge Trail #498 a short way north to the Whistler Cutoff and drop to the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail #478 on the valley floor, about 3.1 miles and 5,280 ft. Follow it north about 4.8 miles to the Eureka Creek Trail and climb along Berk Creek to Fred's Lake (6,507 ft), a common camp. From the lake, cross the crest east into the upper Eureka Creek basin on the faint, unmaintained trail, where the creek can be hard to cross in snowmelt, and continue up into Shellrock Basin on the south side of the Lago-Carru ridge.
trip.itinerary: A common 3-day plan: Day 1 - hike in from the Robinson Creek or Slate Pass trailhead to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin. Day 2 - climb Mount Lago (often combined with Mount Carru via the connecting saddle) from a Shellrock Basin camp, roughly a half-day round trip. Day 3 - hike out. Many parties extend to 4-5 days to add Osceola Peak, Mount Rolo, or a full Pasayten ridge traverse (e.g. via Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain).

waypoints.name: Slate Pass Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From SR 20 at Mazama, follow Lost River Road to the end of the pavement, then the narrow gravel Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) to Harts Pass; trailers are not allowed. At the guard station turn right onto Slate Peak Road (FR 5400-600) and climb about 3.5 miles to the Slate Pass Trailhead at the second switchback beyond the horse loading area, about 6,900 ft. Fill out the free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Pasayten Trail junction
waypoints.directions: Head north on Buckskin Ridge Trail #498 and take the Whistler Cutoff where it splits off, dropping steeply off the ridge to the Middle Fork Pasayten (Robinson Creek) Trail #478 on the valley floor. The slope just below the pass holds snow into summer, and the river here is crossed without a bridge.

waypoints.name: Fred's Lake
waypoints.directions: Turn north and follow the Middle Fork trail down the valley past the first Eureka Creek Trail junction. About 4.8 miles from the Whistler Cutoff, turn east on the Eureka Creek Trail and climb along Berk Creek to Fred's Lake.

waypoints.name: Shellrock Basin camp area
waypoints.directions: From Fred's Lake, climb to the pass on the crest above the lake and drop east into the upper Eureka Creek basin on the faint, unmaintained middle section of the Eureka Creek Trail; the crossing of upper Eureka Creek can be difficult in snowmelt. Continue east and up into Shellrock Basin on the south side of the Lago-Carru ridge.

waypoints.name: Mount Lago Summit
waypoints.directions: Climb north up Lago's broad south slope, leaving the heather for continuous scree, talus and loose rock ribs; there is no path and no single line. Gain the summit ridge and follow the faint boot path along the crest to the true high point, staying back from the north side, which drops off in a huge cliff.

wa_mount_lago_south_slope_south_face.notes: The high start most parties use. From Slate Pass the trail drops north into the Middle Fork Pasayten; follow it down-valley past the Berk Creek junction, then climb to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin to camp. Lago is usually combined with Carru and Osceola.
hazards: Notoriously loose, crumbly rock throughout the upper mountain; rockfall onto parties below
Enormous cliff on the north side of the summit ridge
Awkward crossing of upper Eureka Creek when swollen with snowmelt on the way to camp
Long walk down the Middle Fork Pasayten then back up to Fred's Lake or Shellrock Basin
Open talus and crest give no shelter from thunderstorms; grizzly and black bear country
Unmarked cross-country travel; lingering early-season snow

wa_mount_logan_r1.name: Easy Pass and Fisher Basin
camps: Fisher Creek lake camp below the Banded Glacier
wa_mount_logan_r1.notes:
The usual way in while SR 20 is open. From the Easy Pass Trailhead near milepost 151, climb about 3.5 miles to the 6,500-ft pass, drop into Fisher Basin, and follow the Fisher Creek Trail down the valley — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. About ten miles one way. The trailhead sits inside the highway's winter closure, and the pass is often snowbound until July.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge, sometimes called Christmas Tree Col, which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.
wa_mount_logan_r1.season: July to September; the Easy Pass trail usually holds snow until July
hazards: Gated trailhead tied to SR-20 seasonal closure limits when this way in is open
Crossing of a 6,500 ft pass into Fisher Basin before dropping to the lake camp
Christmas Tree Col may need a rope for steep snow; snow bridge collapse risk on the Banded Glacier
Crevasses on the Banded Glacier; talus over hard glacier ice is treacherous in a whiteout
Cliff bands above the lake camp; loose chossy summit ridge and rockfall in approach gullies
Sustained off-trail route-finding; heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin early season
wa_mount_logan_r1.baseFinding:
The critical transition is a negative test: gain the northeast ridge on solid rock at about 8,800 ft rather than attempting the summit block directly from the glacier. That is the base of the climbing and it is the single thing this route can get wrong. If you are trying to climb off the ice straight at the summit, you have skipped the transition — cross the glacier until you can step onto solid rock on the ridge, and only then start up.

Getting there is a sequence of two cols and they are different things. First, from the lake camp near 5,160 ft, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — and drop over it onto the Banded Glacier. Second, ascend the Banded to the Banded-Douglas Col, which is literally the saddle between the two named glaciers. A col you crossed to reach ice, and a col you reached by climbing ice, are not the same feature.

So the question that settles your position in fog is which glacier is under you: this route travels between two named glaciers, so if you can identify which one you are standing on, you know which stage you are at. The Banded is the one you drop onto from the ridge above camp; the Douglas is on the far side of the col above.

And all three Logan routes end on the same 300 ft of class 3-4 summit block, so the summit confirms nothing. What distinguishes them is entirely below: this one comes from Fisher Creek and a lake camp; the Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder; the Fremont Glacier route comes from Park Creek Pass on the other side of the mountain.

Watch the scree below the glacier on the way up with the descent in mind — it is unstable enough that parties note it climbs far better than it downclimbs.

bivy.name: Neve Camp
bivy.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the bugs are heavy through midsummer. Nothing about it is alpine, which is exactly its function on a corridor where the climbing is fifteen or more miles in.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek runs beside the camp and is reliable all season.

bivy.capacity: Small forested camp, reported at roughly five tent spots, spread out enough that parties are not on top of each other. Confirm the count and per-site party limit when the permit is issued.

waypoints.note: Gain the northeast ridge on solid rock near 8,800 ft rather than climbing straight off the glacier at the summit block. Reverse the route to descend; the scree below the glacier is much harder going down than up.

The longer way in, and the one that stays open all year: the Colonial Creek trailhead is west of SR 20's winter closure gates. Take the Thunder Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground near 1,200 ft about nine miles to the Fisher Creek Trail junction, then the Fisher Creek Trail about three miles, past the handrailed log bridge, to the stream that drains the lake camp near 5,160 ft. The critical transition is a negative test: gain the northeast ridge on solid rock at about 8,800 ft rather than attempting the summit block directly from the glacier. That is the base of the climbing and it is the single thing this route can get wrong. If you are trying to climb off the ice straight at the summit, you have skipped the transition — cross the glacier until you can step onto solid rock on the ridge, and only then start up.

wa_mount_maude_r1.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col
wa_mount_maude_r1.notes: Drive the Chiwawa River Road, FR 62, roughly twenty-two miles and turn right onto the Phelps Creek road, FR 6211, to the trailhead at about 3,500 ft. The trail up the valley is the same tread hikers use for Spider Meadow. Walk the Phelps Creek trail, #1511, about three and a half flat miles to where it meets Leroy Creek near 4,120 to 4,140 ft. Cross on a large tree or by rock-hopping — awkward in early season with the creek up — and pick up the well-worn but unsigned climbers' trail, #1512, on the north side of the creek. It is sometimes called the Carne Mountain High Route, but the two are also treated as different paths, so do not assume the names are interchangeable. It climbs steeply, then eases into the Leroy Creek Basin meadow at about 6,100 ft, roughly five miles from the car and a little over two hours for a party moving well with light packs. Good camping and water. Above the basin, one party continued on the high-route path less than a quarter mile and then went directly into the upper basin below Maude by way of a gully with a small waterfall. Keep climbing cross-country over meadow, scrub, talus and probably snow to the Seven Fingered Jack / Maude col at about 8,150 ft, north-west of Maude's summit.
wa_mount_maude_r1.season: Best while the face still holds continuous snow and ice, roughly Jun into mid-Jul; it used to hold year round and no longer does
hazards: Leroy Creek crossing on a log or by rock-hopping, awkward when running high early season

Sixty-degree snow for the first moves off the traverse; bergschrund at the base of the face
Cornice at the top of the face; pieces have released across parties' tracks
Frequent rockfall as the face warms; very poor rock quality across this group of peaks
Easy to descend a west-side gully by mistake instead of continuing south toward Ice Lakes
wa_mount_maude_r1.baseFinding:
The col is not the route, and that is the thing to internalise before you get there. From the col you have to go down about four hundred feet, and not in one clean line — it comes in a series of forced descents alternating with traverses.

The recorded sequence: from the col, take the option toward the Entiat River valley side, downclimb roughly a hundred feet of face to a moderate bench, traverse a couple of hundred yards, be forced down again, traverse again, and eventually arrive at a steep snow slope beneath an overhang. That slope is the steepest ground of the day, around sixty degrees for the first moves, easing above.

The test is visual and it is unambiguous: you have descended far enough when the face comes into full view. Until it does, you are still traversing. One party took an hour and a half from the col to standing on continuous snow at the foot of the face.

Once on it, the lower face runs around thirty-five to forty degrees. A rib on the right side of the face is the line parties choose, not because it is named but because it keeps you out from under the cornice.

What not to expect: a bergschrund. The 1957 first ascent, coming from below on the Ice Lakes side, stood at a schrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above. Parties arriving by the col traverse enter partway up the face and bypass that ground entirely, and modern reports of this approach do not mention a schrund at all. The hazard people actually record here is the cornice at the top — one party had a piece of it come down and sweep across their tracks.

Honest gap worth knowing: nothing published tells you how to distinguish Maude's north face from Seven Fingered Jack's. The two, with Fernow, form one continuous headwall at the head of the Entiat, so the col is your positional anchor rather than the look of the wall.

On the way down, stay south and descend toward Ice Lakes. Parties regularly drop into one of the gullies cut into Maude's west side, either by mistake or thinking it a shortcut, and it is not.

wa_mount_maude_r1.name: Entiat River and Ice Lakes from the east — the first-ascent line

bivy.name: Upper Ice Lake
bivy.notes: The higher of two lakes in a pumice basin directly under the peak, about a mile and 400 ft above Lower Ice Lake, near the 6,900 ft high point of the Ice Creek trail. Parties climbing the north face camp on the snow-free ground at the lake's south end and start around four in the morning, dropping from the lake onto the slopes beside the face and climbing to the glacier; reckon on about four hours from the edge of the Entiat Glacier to the summit. It can be reached from Leroy Basin by the climbers' path heading south, or from the long Entiat River approach.
bivy.water: The lake, which can still be partly frozen early in the season
bivy.permit: Also in the Glacier Peak Wilderness, with the same free self-issued permit; the standard guidance is to pitch on the pumice and keep off the meadows
bivy.capacity: Open pumice flats with room for several parties, at the south end of the lake

approachLogistics.trailhead: Entiat River Trailhead (Cottonwood, end of Entiat River Road)

wa_mount_maude_r1.notes:
Drive the Entiat River Road and walk the Entiat River trail #1400 about eight and a quarter miles to the Ice Creek trail. The Entiat River has to be crossed on logs, and if there is no log at the trail there may be a large jam south of it.

The first-ascent party did not follow the river to the meadows at its head. They walked instead to the col between Spectacle Buttes and Maude's south-east side and dropped from Ice Lakes onto the slopes beside the face, judging it more direct and free of bushwhacking. That cost them nearly three thousand feet of climbing to reach Ice Lakes.
wa_mount_maude_r1.season: Same window; this side is a much longer walk and is mostly used by parties already camped at Ice Lakes or exiting that way
hazards: Unbridged crossing of the Entiat River on logs; a log jam may stand in for a missing log
Very long walk in on a trail through terrain burned by the 2015 Wolverine Fire
Bergschrund at the foot of the face on this side; crevasse crossing on the Entiat Glacier
Cornice at the top of the face; wet snow sluffing
Frequent rockfall from bordering buttresses as the face warms; variable ice conditions
Poor rock quality throughout; exposure on the face
wa_mount_maude_r1.baseFinding:
The base-finding here is one moment rather than a sequence: after the long grind up to Ice Lakes, you come over the crest and the face is right there in front of you. The first-ascent account says exactly that — the doubts about having picked the right way vanished on cresting the ridge.

Coming from this side you meet the face at its foot rather than partway up, which is the real difference from the col approach. That means descending steep snow slopes to a snowfield, then up to the glacier, and standing at the bergschrund between the glacier and the ice sheet above — around two thousand feet of it on the first ascent, averaging forty to forty-five degrees and over forty-five near the top.

So the test is which problem you are handed. If you are looking up at a schrund at the bottom of the whole face, you came from below. If you never saw one, you came across from the col.
